cue: The view is very wide and soft, and it runs a little slowly.

cpd.note: the finest stripes a honeybee reliably resolved

fov.note: the general figure given for bees

rate.note: the app slows time by a chosen amount to suggest an eye that keeps up with fast flicker

overlay.name: polar
overlay.note: a faint pattern across the sky stands in for the polarized light a bee reads

rows: A honeybee can resolve stripes only as fine as about 0.26 cycles per degree, and a bumblebee about 0.25. A person resolves about 60 cycles per degree, so the picture is very soft.
Bees see about 300 degrees around them on a level plane. In a honeybee each eye reaches 156 degrees back from straight ahead, which leaves only a small blind wedge behind.

Bees have three kinds of colour receptor, for ultraviolet, blue and green, with peaks near 346, 430 and 540 nanometres in the honeybee. They can see ultraviolet light but no far red. This view leaves the colours to the general insect view.
bee.jsonl:German Aerospace Center (DLR) and Bee Sensory and Behavioural Ecology Lab 2026

A honeybee can still follow flicker at about 200 times a second in bright light and 144 times a second at 300 lux. This view runs a little slowly to suggest an eye that catches more moments than ours.

Bees read the pattern of polarized light in the sky as a compass, using ultraviolet receptors in a special strip along the top of the eye and in their three small simple eyes. The faint overlay in this view is a picture of that sense.
How much time slows and how the polarized sky is drawn are the app's choices. Measurements lie behind the ideas but give no exact values for them.
